title: Ọ̀fà (Historical City & Ancient Kingdom)
description: The monumental frontline defensive city and sovereign Ìbọ̀lọ́ kingdom in Kwara State, famed for metallurgical independence, sweet potatoes (Ọ̀fà Ọlọ́rọ̀ Àjẹ́), and warrior king Olúmọdọ̀.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity (c. 14th Century CE): Founded by Olúmọdọ̀, an Ifẹ̀ prince and master hunter-warrior. 19th Century: Functioned as the southern defensive rampart resisting imperial northern incursions during the Ọ̀fà wars (1887-1893). Contemporary: Celebrated educational, railway, and commercial crossroads.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Ọ̀fà' (the swift archer/defender). Philosophically embodies civic fortitude and territorial sanctuary: 'Ọ̀fà kì í jẹ́ kí ogun kọjá lọ sí Ìkòyí' (Offa never allows warfare to reach the inner heartlands).
material_and_craftsmanship: Ancient red-clay defensive ramparts (Odi Ọ̀fà), indigenous bloomery iron arrowheads, and traditional textile weaving looms.
social_and_ritual_context: Presided over by the Ọlọ́fà of Ọ̀fà and high chiefs; home to the sacred Moremi festival honoring the immortal heroine born of Ọ̀fà royal stock.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀fà kì í jẹ́ kí ogun kọjá lọ sí Ìkòyí; Olúmọdọ̀ l’ẹlẹ́jọ̀ tí ń dá ẹjọ́ ọ̀kọ̀. (Ọ̀fà never permits warfare to cross unchecked into Ìkòyí; Olúmọdọ̀ is the rightful judge who arbitrates through the spear. Celebrates Offa as an impenetrable shield of inner Yorùbáland.)
Ọ̀fà ọmọ olórò àjẹ́, ọmọ iṣu tútù tí ń kọ́ ọ̀rọ̀. (Offa, children of sweet bounty, whose prosperous soil yields nourishment that builds generational wealth.)
diaspora_connections: Reflected in Afro-Cuban Lucumí songs honoring warrior settlements and Moremi praise recitations.
geographical_origin: Kwara State (Ìbọ̀lọ́ Cultural Zone, Southern Kwara)
curatorial_guidelines: Distinguish sharply from archery weaponry Ọfà; showcase palace architecture and Moremi shrines.

title: Èkó (Maritime Capital & Cultural Center)
description: The historic maritime capital, island citadel, and vibrant cosmopolitan center of the Yorùbá world, anchoring transatlantic commerce, royal dynastic councils, and pan-African artistic innovation.
historical_timeline: 15th Century: Founded as an Àwórì coastal settlement under Olofin. 16th-17th Century: Transformed into a fortified royal trading port and palace seat (Ìgá Ìdúngànrán) under the Ọba of Lagos. 1861: British annexation and treaty of cession. 20th-21st Century: Megacity and global cultural powerhouse.
etymology_and_philosophy: Dual etymology: from Ẹ̀dó 'Èkó' (fortified war camp) and Yorùbá 'Oko' (agricultural farm settlement). Philosophically represents intense dynamism: 'Èkó àkétè ilé ọgbọ́n' (Lagos, the throne of discernment).
material_and_craftsmanship: Stilt lagoon architecture, Portuguese-Brazilian stone-masonry compounds (Aguda Quarter), and the sacred carved pillars of Ìgá Ìdúngànrán.
social_and_ritual_context: Vibrant arena of the Adámú Òrìṣà (Èyọ̀) festival, royal processions of the Idejo white-cap chiefs, and maritime offerings to Olókun.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Èkó gb’ólé kò gb’ọ̀lẹ, o fi ọmọ lówó o fi ọmọ lẹ́kọ̀ọ́. (Lagos accommodates the industrious but rejects indolence; it enriches one child with fortune while instructing another through rigorous discipline.)
Èkó àkétè ilé ọgbọ́n; ẹni tí kò gbọ́n t’ó dé Èkó, a gbọ́n. (Lagos is the citadel of wisdom; the foolish person who enters its gates must either acquire discernment or become a servant to the astute.)
diaspora_connections: Primary point of return for Brazilian 'Tabom' and Saro returnees in the 19th century, birthing Afro-Brazilian architecture in Lagos Island.
geographical_origin: Lagos Island and Coastline, Southwestern Nigeria
curatorial_guidelines: Strictly prevent homophonic confusion with cornmeal food cake Ẹ̀kọ; highlight coastal lagoon life and Èyọ̀ masquerades.

title: Ìsàlẹ̀ Èkó (Ancestral Island & Core Settlement)
description: The sacred indigenous heart of Lagos Island, housing Ìgá Ìdúngànrán (palace of the Ọba of Lagos), ancestral shrines of the Idejo chiefs, and the spiritual epicenter of the Èyọ̀ masquerade.
historical_timeline: Dating to early 16th century Àwórì-Benin dynastic agreements; preserved through colonial expansion as the sovereign un-ceded heartland of indigenous Lagosians.
etymology_and_philosophy: Literally 'Downtown / Lowland of Èkó', designating the primordial coastal base where lagoon meets the dry island ridge.
material_and_craftsmanship: Historic courtyards, carved royal brass-studded entrance gates, and ancient burial crypts inside family compounds.
social_and_ritual_context: Venue where the Ọba of Lagos performs annual state libations, and where each Èyọ̀ Iga group parades under solemn liturgical chants.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: A kì í mọ̀ ’nkan tí Ọba Èkó ń jẹ, àyàfi bí a bá jẹ́ ọmọ Ìgá. (One cannot divine the feast of the King of Lagos unless one is an initiate of the royal palace—underscoring palace confidentiality and sacred lineage protocols.)
diaspora_connections: Revered by Brazilian returnee families who settled across the Portuguese Quarter bordering Ìsàlẹ̀ Èkó.
curatorial_guidelines: Present historic streetscapes, brass staffs of the Ọba, and tall white Èyọ̀ crowns.

title: Kàbbà (Historic Okun Kingdom & City)
description: The historic cultural and administrative capital of the Okun-Yorùbá people in Kogi State, seat of the Obaro of Kabba and epicenter of indigenous mountain resistance and agrarian excellence.
historical_timeline: 14th Century: Dynastic roots tracing to Ilé-Ifẹ̀ migrations settling among the protective inselbergs. 19th Century: Center of heroic defense against Nupe imperial raiding armies. 20th Century: Educational and administrative hub of Kabba Province.
etymology_and_philosophy: Philosophically signifies high-altitude community vigilance, steadfastness, and cultural autonomy.
material_and_craftsmanship: Granite architectural terraces, handwoven Okun ceremonial cloth (Aṣọ Ìpàpà), and terraced yam cultivation implements.
social_and_ritual_context: Celebrated during the annual Oro festival and the royal installation of the Obaro of Kabba.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọmọ Kàbbà kì í sùn lójú ogun; àpáta tó gbé wa ga ní ń sọ wa d’olókun. (The child of Kabba sleeps not during conflict; the towering rock that elevates our homes makes us kings of the highlands.)
diaspora_connections: Okun linguistic patterns and ancestral proverbs survive in diaspora Lucumí liturgies.
curatorial_guidelines: Highlight mountain topography and traditional woven textiles.

title: Ìjùmú (Ancestral Okun Confederacy)
description: The venerable Okun-Yorùbá confederacy of autonomous towns in Kogi State (Iyara, Ogidi, Iyamoye, Ekinrin-Adde), celebrated for democratic communal governance, granite sanctuaries, and sacred groves.
historical_timeline: Early classical era: Settlements established around ancient caves and monoliths. 19th Century: Ogidi-Ijumú resistance alliances against external cavalry forces.
etymology_and_philosophy: Emphasizes federated harmony and decentralized democracy: autonomous towns bound in mutual defense pacts.
material_and_craftsmanship: Pottery guilds, iron smelting relics, and hand-carved ceremonial staves.
social_and_ritual_context: Annual Ogidi Yam Festival and sacred rites honoring ancestors of the caves.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìjùmú kì í jẹ́ kí àkókò kọjá láì kọ́ ọmọ ní ìwà rere. (Ìjùmú never allows a season to pass without schooling its children in noble character.)
diaspora_connections: Preserved in trans-Saharan and transatlantic oral historical accounts of northern Yorùbá resistance.
curatorial_guidelines: Show monolith formations and festive community processions.

title: Adó-Èkìtì (Ancestral Capital & Seat of the Ẹwí)
description: The paramount sovereign capital of Èkìtì State and royal seat of the Ẹwí of Adó-Èkìtì, famous for the magnificent Ẹwí Palace, rich oral poetry, and leadership in the Ẹ̀kìtìparapọ̀ liberation struggle.
historical_timeline: c. 13th Century CE: Founded by the Ẹwí Awamaro, son of Odùduwà from Ilé-Ifẹ̀. 19th Century: Stood as the political hub during the Kiriji/Ẹ̀kìtìparapọ̀ liberation wars (1877-1893). 1996: Named state capital.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Adó' (settlement/shelter) and 'Ẹwí' (the orator/monarch whose spoken decree is law).
material_and_craftsmanship: Ancient palace courtyards with carved caryatids, monumental gables, and bronze ceremonial implements.
social_and_ritual_context: Epicenter of the annual Udiroko festival (traditional new year), where the Ẹwí blesses the populace.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Adó kò gbọ́dọ̀ dákẹ́ kí Ẹwí má sọ̀rọ̀; ohun tí Ẹwí bá wí ni àṣẹ ìlú. (Adó cannot remain silent when the Ẹwí speaks; whatever the monarch decrees is the law of the commonwealth.)
diaspora_connections: Documented in British archival records and Yoruba diasporic research in Cuba and Brazil.
curatorial_guidelines: Present the royal palace of the Ẹwí and festival assemblies.

title: Ère Ìbejì (Sacred Twin Memorial Effigy)
description: The sacred, intricately carved wooden memorial figure commissioned when a twin passes, serving as a metaphysical vessel through which the immortal spiritual vitality of the deceased child is sustained.
historical_timeline: Antiquity tracing to classical Ọ̀yọ́ and Ẹ̀gbá traditions; heightened during the 18th century as the Yorùbá world developed the highest rate of twin births in humanity.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Ère' (effigy/carving) and 'Ìbejì' (born-two / twin). Anchored in the belief that twins share a single spiritual essence and possess divine power (Àṣẹ) to bring fortune.
material_and_craftsmanship: Carved from sacred Ìrókò or mahogany hardwood, rubbed with red camwood powder (Osùn), adorned with miniature cowrie-shell tunics and brass armlets.
social_and_ritual_context: Bathed, fed, sung to, and clothed regularly by the mother as though living, ensuring familial harmony and balance.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ère Ìbejì kì í kú; ó lọ sí ọjà ni. (The sacred twin effigy never dies; it has merely departed on an errand to the ancestral market—affirming immortality.)
Ẹni tó bí Ìbejì kò gbọ́dọ̀ ráhùn; olówó ọjọ́ wájú l’ọ́mọ. (He who births twins must never utter laments of poverty; twins bring ancestral abundance.)
diaspora_connections: Revered as the 'Ibeji' or 'Jimaguas' in Cuban Santería and 'Ibêji' in Brazilian Candomblé.
geographical_origin: Pan-Yorùbáland (special prominence in Ọ̀yọ́, Ìbàdàn, Abẹ́òkúta)
curatorial_guidelines: Display with proper camwood patina, glass bead necklace, and respectful spiritual framing.

title: Ère Ẹlẹ́gbára (Consecrated Sculptural Icon of Èṣù)
description: The consecrated sculptural wooden or laterite figure representing Èṣù-Ẹlẹ́gbára, characterized by a long backward-curving phallic coiffure, whistles, and cowrie adornments.
historical_timeline: Classical era onwards: Present at palace gateways, crossroads, and household thresholds as the prime divine messenger between humanity and Olódùmarè.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Ẹlẹ́gbára' (the Owner of Dynamic Kinetic Force). Embodies ethical choice, mediation, and divine retribution.
material_and_craftsmanship: Hardwood carving blackened with vegetal dyes, hung with cowrie strands, miniature calabashes, and leather bands.
social_and_ritual_context: Venerated with palm oil (Ẹpo Pupa) at crossroads and shrine entrances before any divine consultation.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Èṣù kì í jẹ́ kí awo tẹ́; ẹni tí ó bọ̀wọ̀ fún Èṣù a ri àlàáfíà. (Èṣù never permits the conscientious initiate to suffer disgrace; whoever honors the gatekeeper finds civic peace.)
diaspora_connections: Widely sculpted as Eleguá heads in Afro-Cuban religion and Exu statues in Brazilian Candomblé and Umbanda.
curatorial_guidelines: Present with backward headcrest, polished surface, and cowrie strings.

title: Ẹyọ Owó (Unit Cowrie Shell Currency)
description: The fundamental unit shell of the historic Yorùbá monetary system, grouped mathematically into strings (Ọgọ́rùn-ún), bundles (Ẹgbàá), and bags (Àpò) for imperial commerce.
historical_timeline: Active for over seven centuries until demonetized by British colonial fiat in the early 20th century.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Ẹyọ' (single unit/grain) and 'Owó' (money/wealth).
material_and_craftsmanship: Glossy porcelain-like white shell of Cypraea moneta with distinct serrated aperture.
social_and_ritual_context: Used for dowry payments, marketplace barter, and liturgical offerings in Ẹsẹ̀ Ifá and Ẹbọ.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹyọ owó kan kì í rún; bí a bá kó o jọ, a di ẹgbàá. (A single cowrie is never discarded; when assembled patiently, it becomes thousands—praising thrift and compounding labor.)
diaspora_connections: Sacred cowries (diloggún) used across Lucumí and Candomblé divination systems.
curatorial_guidelines: Show natural dorsal view and serrated slit.

title: Ikin Ọlọ́jú Mẹ́rin (Four-Eyed Consecrated Palm Nut)
description: The supreme consecrated four-pored palm nut harvested from the sacred Ọ̀pẹ Ifá tree (*Elaeis guineensis*), held by high-priest Babaláwos as the ultimate physical vehicle of Ọ̀rúnmìlà's voice.
historical_timeline: Rooted in the primordial Ifá corpus codified at Ilé-Ifẹ̀; preserved unchanged for millennia.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Ọlọ́jú Mẹ́rin' (possessor of four eyes), symbolizing the four cardinal cosmic directions and complete clairvoyance.
material_and_craftsmanship: Dense, oil-patinated palm nut with four distinct germination pores, polished by decades of herbal infusions.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast in pairs of 16 during Itadogun and Itẹfa initiation rituals on the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ikin ọlọ́jú mẹ́rin kì í purọ́; orí mẹ́rin ni ó fi ń wo ayé. (The four-eyed sacred nut utters no falsehood; with four eyes it surveys the four corners of existence.)
diaspora_connections: Preserved as 'Ikin' in Cuban and Brazilian Ifá lineages.
curatorial_guidelines: Highlight the 4 clear circular pores and dark sacred patina.

title: Ikin Ọlọ́jú Mẹ́ta (Three-Eyed Sacred Palm Nut)
description: The sacred three-pored palm nut from the sacred palm tree, representing specialized metaphysical diagnostics and balance between the spiritual realm, the ancestors, and the living.
historical_timeline: Integral companion in ancient babaláwo divination bags (Àpò Mìníjẹ̀kùn) alongside 4-eyed nuts.
etymology_and_philosophy: Signifies tripartite cosmic harmony: Ọ̀run (Heaven), Ayé (Earth), and Ilẹ̀ (The Underworld/Ancestors).
material_and_craftsmanship: Natural cured botanical palm nut showing three distinct indented apertures.
social_and_ritual_context: Venerated in consultations seeking energetic balance and ancestral appeasement.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọlọ́jú mẹ́ta ló mọ àdàbà orí igi; Ifá mọ ohun tó pamọ́. (He with three eyes discerns the hidden dove in the treetop; Ifá sees that which is invisible to mortal eyes.)
diaspora_connections: Maintained in diaspora divination sets.
curatorial_guidelines: Present alongside three-fold ancestral altar items.

title: Agẹrẹ Ológun (Equestrian Carved Divination Vessel)
description: A magnificent hand-carved hardwood caryatid divination cup supported by a mounted equestrian warrior (Ẹlẹ́ṣin) brandishing weapons, symbolizing martial vigilance and spiritual protection.
historical_timeline: 17th–19th Century: Fluctuation of Ọ̀yọ́ imperial military ethos into liturgical woodcarving masterworks by master sculptors.
etymology_and_philosophy: Equestrian iconography (Ẹlẹ́ṣin) represents imperial command, divine fortitude, and the triumph of wisdom over chaos.
material_and_craftsmanship: Carved from a single block of dense hardwood with polychrome pigments and brass inlays.
social_and_ritual_context: Placed at the right side of the Babaláwo's consultation mat holding the 16 Ikin nuts.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹlẹ́ṣin inú agẹrẹ kì í bọ́; awo tó mọ̀wà ní ń gbé e. (The warrior atop the sacred vessel never falls; only the priest of exemplary character commands its spiritual power.)
diaspora_connections: Prominently featured in international museum collections (The Met, British Museum, Smithsonian).
curatorial_guidelines: Showcase vertical relief, equestrian bridle details, and the cupped vessel above.

title: Agẹrẹ Arúgbá (Kneeling Maiden Caryatid Vessel)
description: An exquisite caryatid divination cup supported by a kneeling female devotee (Arúgbá) holding her breasts or balancing the bowl on her head, personifying devotion, fertility, and cosmic calm (Ètùtù).
historical_timeline: Classical era onwards: Masterpieces carved by Ọ̀yọ́, Òwọ̀, and Ìjẹ̀bú sculptors.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Arúgbá' (she who carries the sacred calabash). Represents unshakeable reverence: 'Ìkúnlẹ̀ ni ti obìnrin' (kneeling is the posture of feminine spiritual grace).
material_and_craftsmanship: Sculpted hardwood rubbed with palm oil and camwood, exhibiting delicate facial scarifications (Kẹ́kẹ́/Gàbàsì).
social_and_ritual_context: Vessel used in high-level royal and societal divination assemblies.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìkúnlẹ̀ arúgbá kì í ṣe ojo; àṣẹ ló ń bọ̀wọ̀ fún. (The kneeling posture of the maiden is not cowardice; it is reverence paid to primordial authority.)
diaspora_connections: Revered in Afro-Cuban and Brazilian Yemọja/Ọ̀ṣun liturgical shrines.
curatorial_guidelines: Highlight symmetrical posture, calm facial expression, and caryatid balance.

title: Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ Agbalagba (Elder Master Divination Chain)
description: The heavy, consecrated divination chain wielded exclusively by veteran elder Babaláwos, strung with eight rare aged seed-pods, brass tokens, and ancestral relics.
historical_timeline: Passed down across multiple generations from master to initiated successor.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Agbalagba' (elder of venerable wisdom). Embodies lifetime mastery of the 256 Odù Ifá.
material_and_craftsmanship: Heavy hand-braided leather cord or copper chain connecting seasoned seed pods backed by ancestral beads.
social_and_ritual_context: Reserved for complex communal consultations, epidemic arbitrations, and king-making rites.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ agbalagba kì í sọ̀rọ̀ lásán; bí ó bá dákẹ́, awo a bẹ̀rù. (The elder divination chain never speaks in vain; when it falls silent, priests re-examine the cosmos.)
diaspora_connections: Preserved in elder Lucumí and Candomblé house lineages.
curatorial_guidelines: Present with dark oiled patina and antique brass links.

title: Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ Idẹ (Sacred Brass Divining Chain)
description: An aristocratic divination chain whose eight half-pods are cast from sacred lost-wax brass (Idẹ), producing resonant acoustic chimes when dropped to summon ancestral attention.
historical_timeline: Popularized in Ìjẹ̀bú and Òwọ̀ brass-working guilds during the 16th–18th centuries.
etymology_and_philosophy: Brass (Idẹ) never rusts nor decays: symbolizes immortal truth and the incorruptibility of divine revelation.
material_and_craftsmanship: Lost-wax cast brass half-pods decorated with geometric chevron and interlace motifs linked by brass chain.
social_and_ritual_context: Utilized in royal courts and Òṣùgbó/Ògbóni ancestral sanctuaries.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Idẹ kì í kànkàn; ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ idẹ kì í d'ègún. (Brass never corrupts into rust; the brass divination chain never degenerates into falsehood.)
diaspora_connections: Survives in Cuban Lucumí and Brazilian Ketu high-priesthood regalia.
curatorial_guidelines: Highlight golden metallic sheen and acoustic chime.

title: Ọpọ́n Ifá Olórí Èṣù (Divination Tray with Crown of Èṣù)
description: The canonical sacred divination tray carved with the high-relief crowned head of Èṣù-Ẹlẹ́gbára at its northern perimeter, looking inward upon the powdered surface.
historical_timeline: Classical era: Standardized across all Yorùbá kingdoms as the primordial cosmogram of consultation.
etymology_and_philosophy: Signifies that Èṣù is the vigilant inspector of cosmic truth, ensuring that what is revealed is honest and true.
material_and_craftsmanship: Seasoned hardwood carved with intricate geometric interlace (Àwọrọ̀) borders framing the central flat plane.
social_and_ritual_context: Oriented toward the rising sun; dusted with Ìyẹ̀rosùn powder where the Babaláwo marks the Odù.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Bí a bá tẹ Ifá sórí ọpọ́n, ojú Èṣù ni a kọ́kọ́ ń kọjú sí. (When Ifá is inscribed upon the tray, it is Èṣù's face that we must first acknowledge; the keeper of the threshold precedes revelation.)
diaspora_connections: Replicated across hundreds of Cuban and Brazilian babaláwo altars.
curatorial_guidelines: Focus on the carved visage of Èṣù at top margin and the concentric border carvings.

title: Ọpọ́n Ifá Gbẹ́rọ́ (Deep Relief Ceremonial Divination Tray)
description: A monumental, deep-dish ceremonial divination tray with elevated multi-tiered perimeter carvings depicting kings, snakes, tortoises, and heraldic beasts.
historical_timeline: Commissioned by sovereign monarchs (Ọba) and titled guild elders from master artists.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Gbẹ́rọ́' (spacious and deeply recessed), symbolizing the vastness of the universe held within sacred boundaries.
material_and_craftsmanship: Monumental circular or oblong hardwood dish carved with multi-scene pictorial narratives.
social_and_ritual_context: Used during major state festivals and royal annual divinations.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọpọ́n ńlá kì í fọ́ sọ́wọ́ awo; gbogbo ayé ló gbà sínú. (The monumental tray never shatters in the priest's hands; it holds the entire universe within its sacred rim.)
diaspora_connections: Prized in transatlantic exhibitions and historic collections.
curatorial_guidelines: Present aerial view showing deep center basin and narrative relief perimeter.

title: Ẹdan Ògbóni (Sanctified Cast Brass Twin Rods)
description: The sacred paired male and female lost-wax cast brass figures linked at the crowns by an iron chain, serving as the supreme judicial emblem, oath-taking implement, and constitutional insignia of the Ògbóni/Òṣùgbó society.
historical_timeline: 9th–12th Century Ilé-Ifẹ̀ origins: Exemplified in the classic metallurgical traditions of Ìjẹ̀bú and Ifẹ̀.
etymology_and_philosophy: The iron core represents unbreakable strength, while the exterior brass represents eternal peace and moral incorruptibility: 'Idẹ kì í baje' (Brass never spoils).
material_and_craftsmanship: Lost-wax cast brass over forged iron spikes, joined by hand-forged iron chain links.
social_and_ritual_context: Driven into the earth during sacred arbitrations; initiates swear binding oaths of truth upon them under penalty of cosmic retribution.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹdan kì í purọ́; ẹni tí ó ba búra èké lórí Ẹdan, ilẹ̀ á mu ú. (The Ẹdan utters no falsehood; whoever swears deceitfully upon Ẹdan shall be claimed by Mother Earth.)
Ọkùnrin àti obìnrin ni Ẹdan; àṣẹ wọn kò ṣeé pín. (Male and female are joined as one in Ẹdan; their joint cosmic authority is indivisible.)
diaspora_connections: Revered in Cuban Cabildos and Brazilian Candomblé Ketu lineages as sacred emblems of judicial earth power.
curatorial_guidelines: Display both figures standing joined by chain, emphasizing male/female complementarity.

title: Ìyàwó Titun (The Newly Wedded Bride)
description: The newly wedded bride arriving at her husband's ancestral compound (Agbo-Ilé), celebrated with ceremonial foot-washing rituals (Wíwẹ̀ Ẹsẹ̀), ancestral blessings, and protective choral escorts.
historical_timeline: Classical antiquity: The matrimonial threshold rites transitioning a maiden into an honored partner and future matriarch.
etymology_and_philosophy: Signifies renewal, lineage continuity, and the introduction of new spiritual vital energy into the clan.
material_and_craftsmanship: Adorned in opulent handwoven Aṣọ Òkè (Sányán or Aláárì), coral beads (Ìyùn), and fragrant camwood body ointment.
social_and_ritual_context: Received at the compound entrance by senior wives who wash her feet with water and coins symbolizing peace and prosperity.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹsẹ̀ tí ìyàwó titun fi wọlé, àlàáfíà ló ń mú wá. (The foot with which the new bride enters the compound brings peace and abundant blessings to the lineage.)
diaspora_connections: Ceremonial bridal songs preserved in Lucumí oral literature and wedding celebrations.
curatorial_guidelines: Display traditional foot-washing ceremonial bowl, coral beads, and handwoven head-ties.

title: Ọkọ Ìyàwó (The Matrimonial Bridegroom)
description: The matrimonial husband/bridegroom who prostrates before his bride's family during the Idána ceremony, accepting solemn spiritual and material stewardship of the union.
historical_timeline: Codified through centuries of Yorùbá customary law and Ifá marriage protocols.
etymology_and_philosophy: Represents honorable stewardship, domestic leadership, and protective covenant.
material_and_craftsmanship: Attired in three-piece Aṣọ Òkè Agbádá, Bùbá, and Ṣòkòtò with embroidered Fìlà.
social_and_ritual_context: Flanked by his age-mates and paternal elders as he formally pays respects to his in-laws.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọkọ tó mọyì aya rẹ̀ kì í fi ojú ẹgàn wò ó lójú àlejò. (The husband who honors his wife never diminishes her dignity before strangers.)
diaspora_connections: Customary respect and prostrations preserved in diaspora Yoruba cultural ceremonies.
curatorial_guidelines: Present in formal ceremonial Agbádá regalia with ancestral walking staff.

title: Bàbá Ilé (Patriarch & Head of the Compound)
description: The senior patriarch and judicial custodian of the extended family compound (Agbo-Ilé), responsible for resolving domestic disputes, allocating ancestral farmlands, and leading daily prayers to the ancestors.
historical_timeline: Foundational cornerstone of Yorùbá civic urbanization and compound organization since classical times.
etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Bàbá' (father) and 'Ilé' (house/compound). Symbolizes unshakeable stability, patience, and fair arbitration.
material_and_craftsmanship: Occupies the central veranda (Òdè) overlooking the courtyard; keeper of ancestral staff (Ọ̀pá Àgbà).
social_and_ritual_context: Pours morning water libations to the earth and conducts lineage family assemblies.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Bí bàbá ilé bá wà nílé, olè kì í wọ àgbàlá. (When the father of the compound is present, chaos and theft never breach the courtyard.)
diaspora_connections: Preserved in the structure of Brazilian 'Terreiro' and Cuban 'Casa Templo' elder leadership.
curatorial_guidelines: Show elder seated on ancestral bench in traditional courtyard.
